reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Combines a mandibulofacial dysostosis resembling Treacher Collins with preaxial (thumb-side) upper limb defects
Facial features include malar and mandibular hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, and external ear anomalies
The distinguishing limb finding is preaxial radial ray involvement, with hypoplastic, absent, or triphalangeal thumbs and radial deficiency
Severe micrognathia frequently causes neonatal airway obstruction and feeding difficulty
Cleft palate and velopharyngeal problems are common and contribute to speech difficulty
Most cases are caused by variants in SF3B4, a component of the spliceosome, usually arising de novo
Cognition is generally preserved, so early airway and hearing management strongly influences outcome
reference.pathophysiology: Nager syndrome is a spliceosomopathy, most often caused by loss-of-function variants in SF3B4, which encodes a protein of the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complex essential for pre-messenger RNA splicing. Disturbed splicing during embryogenesis is thought to impair the proliferation and survival of cranial neural crest cells populating the first and second branchial arches, producing the mandibulofacial dysostosis. The same molecular disturbance affects developing limb buds on the preaxial (radial) side, giving rise to thumb and radial ray malformations. This combined facial and appendicular pattern places Nager syndrome among the acrofacial dysostoses, distinguished from Miller syndrome by the preaxial rather than postaxial limb involvement.
additionalDifferentials: Treacher Collins syndrome (facial features without radial limb defects)
Holt-Oram syndrome (radial defects with cardiac disease)
Fanconi anaemia with radial ray anomalies
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the upper limbs to characterise radial ray and thumb anomalies
Audiological assessment for conductive hearing loss
Craniofacial imaging to plan reconstruction and airway management
Sleep study to evaluate obstructive sleep apnoea
Feeding and swallowing assessment in the neonatal period
redFlags: Severe micrognathia causing life-threatening neonatal airway obstruction
Feeding failure requiring supported or non-oral nutrition
Recurrent aspiration from combined palatal and airway abnormality
Anticipated difficult intubation at any procedure
reference.prognosis: Early mortality relates chiefly to airway compromise; those who survive the neonatal period with secure airway and feeding generally have normal intellect and function reasonably well with staged craniofacial and hand reconstruction.
pitfalls: Confusing Nager (preaxial) with Miller syndrome (postaxial) limb involvement
Underestimating neonatal airway risk in the presence of severe micrognathia
Assuming intellectual disability when cognition is typically normal
Overlooking hearing loss and its effect on language
Failing to arrange genetic counselling for de novo dominant recurrence risk
